result:
There is a specific kind of quiet that only exists at 6:13 in the morning.

It is not the quiet of night. Night has a heavy, weighted quiet, full of things sleeping. The quiet of 6:13 is thin and expectant. It is the quiet of a stage five minutes before the curtain, of a kitchen before anyone has decided to make coffee, of a world that has been briefly returned to its factory settings.

I like being awake for it. Not because I am disciplined. I am not. I like it because for a few minutes, nobody wants anything from you. Your phone, if you haven't touched it yet, doesn't know you're alive. The emails haven't found you. The news hasn't started shouting. You exist for a little while without being a participant. You are just an observer with socks on.

And if you observe closely, you notice how much of the world is held together by things no one asked to be noticed for.

Take the sidewalk. I walk the same loop most mornings, and there is a section where the concrete slabs have been lifted by the roots of a maple tree that was planted, probably, in the 1970s by someone who is no longer around. Every year the bump gets a little bigger. Every year, someone comes out with a can of bright orange spray paint and draws a neat triangle around it, so you don't trip. I have never seen this person. I have no idea what department they work for. I have never thought to thank them. But for three years, that anonymous orange triangle has been the only thing between me and a faceplant.

Most of civilization works like that.

We talk a lot about inventors and leaders and disruptors and founders, people who build the big visible things. But the reason the big visible things don't collapse is because there is an army of people doing maintenance on reality. Someone is checking the tension on the cables of the bridge you drove over today. Someone is replacing the rubber seal inside the door of the grocery store freezer so the ice cream stays frozen. Someone is vacuuming the carpet in the airport at 4 a.m. so the first travelers of the day feel like they're starting somewhere clean and plausible.

I once read that in the New York City subway system, there is a team whose entire job is to hunt for water leaks. They walk the tunnels with flashlights, listening. Water is the ancient enemy of tunnels. It always wants back in. Their job is to say, "Here, here is where it is trying to get in." Without them, the city would slowly fill up like a bathtub.

There is something deeply moving to me about that kind of work. It is not work that gets a TED Talk. It is work that says: I will keep this from falling apart while you are busy doing other things.

We live, right now, in a culture that is obsessed with making new things. New apps, new ideas, new identities, new takes. Making is glamorous. Maintenance is not. But maintenance is 90% of life. You don't just have a friendship, you maintain a friendship. You don't just have health, you maintain health. You don't just have knowledge, you maintain it or it decays into trivia. Entropy is the default. Everything wants to become a messy room.

I think about my grandmother's house. She lived in the same house for 52 years. It was never a fancy house. It was a small, sensible house with aluminum siding the color of butter. But it was impeccably maintained. Every spring she would wash the windows inside and out, with newspaper, which actually works. Every fall she would have the furnace serviced, even when money was tight. When the linoleum in the kitchen started to curl, she had it re-glued before it could become a trip hazard. Nothing ever got to the point of crisis. Because she believed in small interventions early.

We have lost some of that wisdom, culturally. We wait until the linoleum is a disaster and then we post about it. We wait until we are burnt out, and then we take a dramatic vacation. We wait until the bridge is falling down, and then we argue about who should have fixed it.

What would happen if we revered maintenance a little more?

I spent a year learning to make sourdough bread, like everyone else did during that strange pocket of time. What they don't tell you on Instagram is that sourdough is not really about making bread. It's about maintaining a starter. That little jar of bubbling paste in your fridge is a colony of living things that will die if you ignore it. You have to feed it. You have to pay attention to its moods. In the summer it gets hyperactive and sour. In the winter it gets sluggish. If you are patient with it, it will make you beautiful bread forever. If you neglect it, it develops a dark liquid on top called hooch and smells like regret.

A lot of things in life have hooch. Your houseplants. Your second language. That novel you were writing. They don't die all at once. They just quietly develop hooch while you are scrolling.

I think the secret, if there is one, is to choose a few things and decide, on purpose, that you will be the person who maintains them.

For me, it's become a short list. My health, which I used to treat like a rental car. My relationships with about five people. My apartment, which is not large but I try to keep in a state where I would not be embarrassed if someone knocked unexpectedly. And my curiosity. That last one is the most demanding starter of them all.

Curiosity needs feeding too. If you don't feed it, it doesn't die, exactly, but it gets replaced by something cheaper, which is certainty. Certainty is fast food for the brain. It feels satisfying in the moment, but it leaves you kind of calcified. Curiosity says, "Huh, I wonder why the orange triangle guy chose that shade of orange." Certainty says, "The city is wasting money again."

I am trying, in my small way, to be a maintenance worker for my own attention. Every morning for those few minutes at 6:13, before the demands roll in, I try to notice one thing that is being quietly kept alive for me.

This morning it was the streetlights. They were still on, though the sky was already pale blue. Each one had a tiny photocell on top that in a few minutes would say, "Okay, that's enough, we can rest now," and they would all click off at once. Someone designed that. Someone installed that. Someone will replace it when it fails.

Someone kept the light on for me, so I could see the sidewalk and the orange triangle and the maple root underneath, all of them doing their slow, patient work of lifting, warning, and growing.

And for a thousand words, that was enough to think about.
